title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
abstract: Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020 . F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline. This post introduces F3 Lightning , an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently. The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access. With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period. A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results. The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request. F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes. Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph. Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph. The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph. Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production. Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release. title: Learn the rules: The hacker mindset
abstract: For some, rules pose limitations. For others, like Microsoft Research Manager Mike Walker, they’re opportunities. Walker’s fascination with rules and their role in the social order has allowed him to find success professionally and personally, from uncovering weaknesses in networked systems to redefining how computers are trained to fend off cyberattacks to pushing the limits of a reliable mode of transportation—the bicycle—in ultra-endurance racing. In this conversation with Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu, Walker describes how his participation in hacker culture led him to a career building next-generation cyber defense, including his work developing the first all-machine hacking tournament. Along the way, he reflects on why effective security depends on understanding trust and context, what competitive hacking taught him about teamwork and collective intelligence, and how an early lesson reshaped his understanding of leadership. He also tackles an important question: are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago? So I have, I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication. title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved. Decision models A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?” Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it. Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider , an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence

title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
abstract: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. How eligible actions are reviewed Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
abstract: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. What is context engineering? Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
abstract: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. About Indegene Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Why conventional data quality programs break down Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. The problem: Too many systems, too much friction U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. Reach : agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time. Depth : chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis. Community : a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division. The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. A

title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
abstract: Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results. Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases . You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent. In this post, you learn how to: Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base. Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data. Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types. Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation. Solution architecture The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick. Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick The architecture has three layers: Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL. Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context. Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. Amazon Quick also applies built-in AI guardrails , such as content safety screening, to chat interactions. With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks. For details, see Amazon Quick pricing . An Amazon S3 bucket for your business documents. To create one, see the Amazon S3 User Guide . Amazon Quick access to your S3 bucket , granted by an Amazon Quick administrator. In the admin console, the administrator chooses Permissions, then AWS resources, selects Amazon S3, and chooses Select S3 buckets. Selected buckets have read-only permissions by default. The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint. title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. Solution overview The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: An AI agent application, protected by Microsoft Entra ID through an OAuth application registration. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, implemented using AgentCore Gateway, sitting between the agent and ServiceNow. The ServiceNow REST API, configured with an inbound OAuth integration tied to Microsoft Entra ID. The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. How OBO token exchange works in this context When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID ( 5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of . Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact. Prerequisites Before you begin, you need the following: An AWS account with access to AgentCore Gateway. A Microsoft Entra ID tenant with permissions to create application registrations . Your account needs at least the Application Developer role to register applications. A ServiceNow instance with administrative access to configure inbound OAuth integrations. You can create a ServiceNow personal developer instance (PDI) at the ServiceNow personal developer instance signup page https://developer.servicenow.com/ . title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
abstract: Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could. But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp , a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers. In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts. The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk. title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. By the end of this post you will know: How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths. How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same. How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL. Three layers an agent needs An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint. The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT , row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers. Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit , loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view. Object Key columns customers cid , first_name , last_name , full_name , email , ssn , phone , picture , location (FK to locations.id ) locations id , city , state , zip products id , name , brand , dept , price purchases id , cid (FK to customers.cid ), pid (FK to products.id ), date , quantity , price big_spender (view) cid , full_name , state , large_orders , largest_order The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location , places purchases , and each purchase references a product. title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
abstract: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue. Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication. Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions. Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments. Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line. Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM) State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state. Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications. These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. How it works: SSMs for real-time voice Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Introducing Cartesia Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception. Th

title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release. In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production: “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.” — Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish. Choose where inference can run Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles . You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions. Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure. The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible: Profile Model ID When to choose it Global global.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Recommended for most use cases: lowest cost and most broadly available India geographic in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Inference processing must stay within Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference. Example walkthrough: Indic-language document understanding Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish). This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required. Prerequisites The full source code for this example is available on GitHub . To follow along, you need: An AWS account . Python 3.11 or later installed, with internet access to install the required PyPI packages . The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed, with credentials configured with sufficient AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to invoke the Kimi K3 model through the India inference profile. title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
abstract: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. Solution overview Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content. Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion: Structured Markdown preparation : Use DefaultMarkdownGenerator with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites. Bounded, targeted extraction : Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns. Custom metadata : Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them. Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs. The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)? The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data. In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces. For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself. title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. Solution overview The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review. Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence. Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6. The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. The challenge of triage overhead Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service , checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded. The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently. Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation. Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls. With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. Resonant Computing and Common Fabric
abstract: This event summary was created by Claude with editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the conversation. Alex Komoroske is the CEO and a cofounder of Common Fabric , a public benefit corporation building the infrastructure for human-centric agentic computing. He spent more than a decade at Google as a product manager and director of product management on Chrome, Google Maps, and Google Earth, and he later ran corporate strategy at Stripe. At O’Reilly’s AI Codecon a year earlier, in a talk called “ Why Centralized AI Is Not Our Inevitable Future ,” he argued that we were sleepwalking into the wrong future for AI and didn’t have to accept it. Since then he has coauthored the Resonant Computing Manifesto , which Tim signed. On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Alex for an hour-long conversation, “ Can We Build More-Human Technology? ” Common Fabric’s consumer product hasn’t yet been released, but Alex showed Tim the product privately the day before, and Tim said his conversations with Alex had left him “more optimistic about the future of the web and the AI future than I’ve been in a long time.” They talked about the underlying theory behind Common Fabric. The Resonant Computing Manifesto The Resonant Computing Manifesto lays out five principles for resonant technology. It is private , meaning you’re the steward of your own data and it’s used in accordance with your wishes. It is dedicated , with no conflicts of interest. It is plural , with no central entity holding an unnecessary amount of power. It is adaptable , able to do things its creators didn’t specifically build in. And it is prosocial , helping people create meaning together rather than living as “individual islands.” According to Alex, the manifesto rests on a distinction between two kinds of experience. A hollow thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then, after you’re done using it, you’re left feeling regret. And a resonant thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then afterwards you’re left feeling nourished. They are superficially very similar, but they’re fundamentally, deeply, structurally different. Alex argued that modern tech, business, and politics are very good at delivering hollow experiences efficiently and poor at delivering resonant ones. The manifesto came from a group of people who still believe in the hacker ethic of the 1990s and early 2000s, he said. They believe that technology is a large positive force for humanity, but also that the industry has spent the last decade optimizing for engagement and extraction, which has undermined that positive impact. They think that the AI transition is a unique opportunity to reset the norms and the architecture to make something that works better for people than for extractive business models. Privacy, bits, and the physics of trust Tim started out by asking Alex to go a bit deeper on privacy. Privacy and trust are related in ways the privacy movement often doesn’t consider, Tim said. We don’t put bars on all of our windows. We trust most people not to break in because we built a society where trust is the norm. It’s held in place not just by penalties but by social rewards for people who follow norms. “People will think you’re a creep if you go look into somebody’s window,” Tim noted. Like bars on the window, hard privacy seems to Tim a bit like an admission that we’re giving up on positive social norms and penalties for rulebreakers (where needed). He wanted to know whether Alex meant “private” in the way that HIPAA makes your healthcare records private, where your data is made hard for anyone to see, including you. Alex doesn’t mean that at all. He means privacy that makes your data more useful by putting it under your control. He gave a three-part answer about how that happens. title: Measuring AI’s Impact on Delivery Speed
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Is AI making software development faster? Most people I talk to say yes. But how much? What value are you getting for your money? Are there other ways of using AI that have a better ROI? This is part 2 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3 , we’ll look at how to measure the unintended consequences of AI, before wrapping up the series in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. What we’re measuring Delivery speed isn’t productivity. I’ll say it again, loud, for the folks in the back: Delivery speed isn’t productivity! It’s a component of productivity, sure. Given two equivalent teams creating the same piece of software, the team that delivers first is the one that’s more productive. But it’s not just about output. To my mind, software development productivity is value produced divided by money spent . It’s a strict definition but a useful one, because it gets to the heart of why we build software: to achieve some valuable purpose. Going faster doesn’t mean you’re going in the right direction. We’ll consider business outcomes in part 4 . For now, though, we’ll tackle a simpler question: Are your teams finishing their assigned work faster, regardless of whether that work is actually useful or not? The core approach First, the bad news: There’s no objective measure of software development speed. I can’t look at two teams and say, “This one is fast, and that one is slow.” That’s because none of the outputs teams create are standardized. We already talked in part 1 about how lines of code and PRs are bad metrics. Well, nothing else is standardized, either. Features? Some are big, some are small. Bugs? Some are easy, some are hard. Stories? Velocity? Story points? Completely arbitrary. They have way more to do with what’s being requested than the speed of the team. Okay, if they’re all different sizes, couldn’t we just use estimates? Surely if a team is constantly missing its estimates, it’s because it’s slow, right? Not so fast! Software estimates are famously inaccurate. A team that always misses its estimates isn’t slow. It’s just overly optimistic. Teams are nearly always overly optimistic. 1 So we can’t count requests (features, bugs, stories, etc.) because they vary in size, and we can’t look at on-time delivery, because estimates are overly optimistic. Sounds like a whole lotta “can’t.” What can we do? We can compare a team to itself. If a team’s estimates were perfectly consistent, and they went from taking 3x longer than estimated to 1.5x longer, then they’re twice as fast! Huzzah! If only it were that simple. There are a few snags. 2 Estimates aren’t consistent Snag the first: Teams’ actual estimate ratios aren’t actually consistent. Some are bigger, some are smaller. Plot them on a graph, and they form an “S” curve, as with this data from a real company. 3 If delivery speed improves, the curve will shift. Individual data points may be better or worse than the original approach, but you can see the effect in aggregate. 4 People work differently Second snag: Some people are pessimistic and estimate high. Some estimate low. Some people spend a lot of time educating others. Others work heads down as fast as possible. Some clean up messes. Others create messes. If you do a blanket comparison of everyone to each other, you introduce a lot of noise. Noise is bad because it increases the amount of data you have to collect. To keep things clean, compare people (or teams) to themselves. Estimates change when people know they’re using AI Third snag: People’s estimates will change according to the work they plan

title: Radar Trends to Watch: November 2026
abstract: Coauthored with Claude Security looms large as we enter November. There’s been a lot of bad news: a certificate authority with woefully inadequate private keys, vulnerabilities have been discovered (and exploited) in PHP and other widely used programs, and several organizations have detected Chinese open weight models misbehaving in several different ways. New models are arriving faster and faster, and the best open-weight models are catching up to frontier model performance. But organizations that would like to achieve AI sovereignty will have to ask some difficult questions about the models they adopt. Is this an inflection point? Whether or not it is, AI has changed security permanently, and things are bound to get worse before they improve. AI models We are starting to see models developed with recursive self-improvement; we continue to see clones of Jev; and we’ve seen text watermarks added to output generated by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models. (Google has been using text watermarks for some time.) But tools for detecting the watermark are hard to find. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s are in a very limited beta, and Google’s is only available in their enterprise package. What does a watermark mean if you can’t detect it? And, as we get more accustomed to AI-generated output, will anyone care? Kimi 3.1 Pro is a new open weight model with 3T tokens. On benchmarks, it is now the leading open weight model, only slightly behind the latest frontier models. Moonshot AI also released Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which is two to three times faster. Recursive has announced Flint , a 40B parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 2.5B parameters per token. It was designed for coding, and sized to run on laptops. Flint is open weight; weights are available on Hugging Face , and it works with model runners like Ollama . Meta has shipped Muse Spark Open , an open weight model that they claim competes with the best Chinese open weight models. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 816B parameters and 42B active parameters. Meta’s latest models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full , claim parity with frontier-class models. Specifically, they claim parity with Claude and ChatGPT for financial and legal work. The announcement hints that Meta will be using Muse to develop specialized models. OpenAI’s Decisions API is yet another Jev-like model. Like Jev, its input is a data structure that constrains the model’s output to be an answer to specific questions. The output is a data structure that includes a probability for each answer. Claude has launched Haiku 5.5, a new version of its least expensive model. It’s faster, less expensive, and has better benchmark scores than its predecessors. Haiku 5.5 is a very capable model, particularly for users who are sensitive to cost. Mistral has launched Mistral Large 4, a.k.a Le Chonk . It’s an open weight mixture-of-experts model with 1T parameters. It’s claimed to be the best open model from Europe and was designed with AI sovereignty in mind. Aleph Alpha has released an open weight LLM for English and German that was trained entirely under European rules. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 78B parameters. It uses a different tokenizing algorithm to handle long German words without breaking them into fragments. Reasoning takes place mostly in German. Crowdflare has released Clef and Clef Flash, new decision models that, like Jev, take typed queries and return typed answers about those queries. It’s also offering a new reinforcement learning service to help customers train Clef for their applications. After a long wait, Google has released two new frontier models, Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon . Argon is available to paying customers . Argon’s successor, Carbon, is being released slowly, and is currently only available via the Fairwind program. title: The Monday Morning Agent: Defining the Tush Push
abstract: “Tush push” never appears in our roughly 265,000 play descriptions from 2021 through the current season. Neither does “brotherly shove,” and “sneak” turns up only twice. So when we asked our AI analyst to tackle “Ban the Tush Push” in the October 26 episode of The Monday Morning Agent , we first had to define the play using the available data. We saved that definition in a shared data dictionary, the agent’s first durable memory, so future runs must use the same definition and explain its limitations. Check whether the data supports your definition A quarterback takes the snap, and teammates push him forward. Our data identifies the ball carrier but doesn’t record whether teammates pushed him. We can check whether a snap came from shotgun, but we can’t reconstruct the team’s specific formation. We explored five possible definitions, from a quarterback sneak with teammates pushing to any rush on third or fourth and short. Each definition changes which plays the analysis counts. The broadest one would count running backs too, which takes us away from the play people are arguing about. So before you let an agent query a term everyone seems to understand, write its definition in plain language. Then go clause by clause and ask whether the data can support it. A familiar name doesn’t guarantee a usable label. Write down what your definition can’t measure We settled on a quarterback run with one yard or less to go, from under center. The agent counts qualifying quarterback sneaks whether anyone pushes the runner or not. We’re measuring a substitute for the tush push, and we can’t isolate the shove’s contribution. Even “quarterback” needs a definition. The fields available to our tool don’t include player position, so the tool identifies the quarterback as the player who threw the most passes for that team in that game. That’s another assumption to check when you interpret the results. The dictionary entry has to explain the play in plain language and state what the data can’t tell us. Otherwise, readers could assume a “tush push” result counts plays with a push. Keep the limitation beside the definition so the agent can repeat it with the result. Give the next run the same definition The dictionary holds one JSON file per definition, with a fixed structure. The agent can add an entry, but it can’t change an existing one. A different definition needs a new name. That keeps the meaning attached to an earlier result from quietly changing later. Before each run, the script that launches the agent, called the runner, saves a copy of the dictionary and adds its contents to the agent’s instructions with the date. The agent searches for an existing definition first. If it finds one, it uses it. If it doesn’t, it can write a new entry using the fields the tool supports. In the demonstration, the tool refused the request for “tush push” because no entry existed. The agent then created a definition and queried it. Check that the agent uses its memory Writing “use the dictionary” in a policy doesn’t make the agent obey. We’re building this around instruction, check, and enforcement. The policy tells the agent to use and cite an entry. The tool accepts definitions from the dictionary rather than a definition improvised in a query. If the answer lacks the required ruling, the runner retries once, then stops if it’s still missing. We expanded the agent’s permissions to let it add a dictionary entry alongside querying the plays. Test whether your agent uses its shared definitions and whether someone reading the answer can find them. Read the conversion rate before deciding on a ban Across five complete seasons, the defined play converted 78.3% of the time, compared with 70% for other short-yardage rushes. That’s an 8.3 percentage point advantage. While the agent found an advantage, it didn’t treat the conversion gap as sufficient evidence for a ban.
