title: Practical Loop Engineering
abstract: The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. The way that I typically work is I have anywhere between five and ten agents working at the same time in parallel. There are going to be some tasks that I’m very happy to delegate fully to agents, as long as I have a very clear idea of the stopping conditions and the constraints around them. And then there are going to be some tasks where I am going to want to keep a closer eye on and code-review what the agent is doing. You’ve probably heard about loop engineering . I talked about it a couple of months ago when I wrote a big blog post about it. A loop is an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results, and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met. There are now basically two core primitives you can think about. In Claude Code you have a goal primitive , which can drive a single bounded task forward until you’ve got a particular goal, like a measurable finish line that’s been met. And then loop reruns on a timer or a fixed interval, so you can use it to schedule changes. Before the primitives were primitives I remember back before we had primitives baked into Claude Code and Codex: Loop engineering was heavily about setting up your own bash loop, a hand-rolled thing. That’s how I approached it. And you might remember earlier in the year, a number of us were playing around with the Ralph loop by Geoff Huntley. We were experimenting, we were sharing our workflows, we were sharing what worked and what didn’t, but it was largely on some of our personal projects where, if we ran into a wall, it didn’t really have a big cost to us. And as we’ve tried to see what patterns and what aspects of loop engineering are now a little bit more baked, I think we have a clearer idea of how you babysit it. I can now largely rely on the output of the primitives in Claude Code and Codex. We’ve come a little way. But at the same time we need to be very diligent, because loop engineering, where you kind of leave it sitting alone and haven’t really thought about whether the end goal or the constraints have been well defined, can leave you in a problematic state. This is why there’s nuance when deciding to use it for an evergreen codebase without users or without as much historical complexity as a brownfield bank codebase. How the Claude Code team frames loops The Claude Code team published their take on four kinds of loops, and it lines up with how I use the primitives ( their write-up ). Before we get to it, here’s my quick summary: On the Claude Code team, we define loops as agents repeating cycles of work until a stop condition is met. We categorize a few different types of loops based on how they are triggered, how they are stopped, what Claude Code primitive is used, what type of task is most appropriate for each. Not all tasks require complex loops; start with the simplest solution and use these patterns selectively. Every prompt you send starts a manual loop with you directing each turn. Claude gathers context, takes action, checks its work, repeats if needed, and responds. We call this the agentic loop. For example, ask Claude to create a “Like” button. It reads your code, makes the edit, runs the tests, and hands back something it believes works. You then manually check the work, and write the next prompt. Their write-up walks each rung. On goal-based loops: Sometimes, a single turn is not enough, especially for more complex tasks. Agents do better when they can iterate. You can extend how long Claude keeps iterating by defining what done looks like with /goal. When you define the success criteria, Claude doesn’t have to make a determination on what is “good enough” and end the loop early. title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
abstract: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. Local officials

title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
abstract: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago. While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level. Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before. What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto. So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election. There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process. The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump. With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat. Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef . —Meghan McCarron This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones. Find out how the sight-restoring implant works . —Linda Marsa MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess . title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
abstract: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
abstract: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood. A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms). Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically. The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer. A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says. During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier. Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center). The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government. It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”). But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet. So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language. The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3. But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents

title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
abstract: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context. Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive. Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents. title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
abstract: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. title: How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses
abstract: The first time Mutembei Kariuki thought about how AI models could work in Kenya, his home country, was in 2019. He was attending a conference at the University of Tokyo on the future of AI, and kept hearing about how this technology was going to transform the world. “But nobody mentioned Africa at all,” he says. Even then—before AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic had launched their chatbots to the public—Kariuki could see significant obstacles to AI adoption in Africa. Internet access was slow and unequal, computing resources for training models were scarce, and there was little high-quality, structured training data. Most people, meanwhile, reached the internet through outdated, low-memory cellphones rather than computers or high-end phones. Together with cofounders Jude Mwenda and Stephanie Njerenga , Kariuki created Fastagger , a startup that builds AI models that can run offline and on low-power cellphones. Its first big product, Auni, is a business-intelligence assistant that launched in 2024; it got a big push when it was integrated into the business app of M-Pesa , Kenya’s largest mobile money service. Since then, about 6,000 businesses have signed up. Auni helps small and medium businesses like barbershops, restaurants, and small manufacturers analyze their transaction data and gives them marketing recommendations. Peter Chege, owner of a salon and barbershop in Nairobi, started using Auni last year. Before that, he recorded all his sales on paper. “We were not able to translate that information into a graph,” he says. Now, the app helps him identify his busiest days and hours, as well as his loyal customers. If a regular customer stops coming, for example, he can send a personalized message encouraging them to return. Fastagger is part of an emerging effort to build AI around the technological realities of users in developing economies, rather than adapting products designed for wealthier markets. In Fastagger’s case, that meant finding a way to make their models work despite inexpensive phones, unreliable internet connections, and business records that may consist of little more than mobile-money transactions. Designing AI for Kenya’s Small Businesses Before developing Auni, Kariuki and his cofounders started by tackling the problem of data availability for AI training. They asked themselves: “How do we get Africa to catch up fast? How do we create training data fast enough, and then how do we actually get it into people’s hands fast enough?” Mutembei Kariuki cofounded Fastagger to develop AI systems that can run offline and on basic phones. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft They decided to focus on mobile phones, and specifically on mobile money apps. With more than 80 percent of Kenya’s adults using them, they offer a rich source of data. One of Fastagger’s first steps was to adapt an open-source optical character recognition (OCR) model to read financial statements produced by mobile money apps. Existing models struggled with the low quality of the PDFs, which had unfamiliar formatting and sometimes contained stamps and errors. And because Fastagger’s prospective users often had unreliable internet connections, they made sure that key steps, like organizing the extracted data into tables, could run on-device. Once they had a model that could process these documents, they began exploring how that structured financial data could help businesses. They spent entire days watching small-business owners work and interact with their customers. One challenge quickly became clear: Owners had little time or resources to think beyond day-to-day operations. “They are standing up the whole day cutting hair,” Kariuki says of salon owners, who are now among Auni’s main users. “You have to think about that dynamic of the user journey, and how they live, and what will be going on in the background.” The Fastagger app helps salon owner Peter Chege better manage his time and keep track of loyal customers. title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
abstract: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM , SSDs , and GPUs . Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance . That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips. title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
abstract: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. Wielding DarkSword One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it. Read full article Comments

title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
abstract: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: the project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using. This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down ten such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity. Read full article Comments

title: VMware releases vSphere Express for virtualization on up to 128 cores
abstract: After alienating many long-time small- to medium-sized business (SMB) customers, Broadcom’s VMware is trying to appeal to its smaller customers. Today, the virtualization company announced vSphere Express, a lower-end virtualization offering for organizations that require “cost-effective essential virtualization.” vSphere Express comes after many customers reported that VMware was pushing them to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), the flagship private cloud bundle that has many features SMBs don’t need and is expensive. Some SMB users have reported that VMware sales representatives previously told them that vSphere Standard, VMware's prior entry-level virtualization offering, wasn’t available anymore. Read full article Comments

title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
abstract: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company's gaming segment cratered. AMD CFO Jean Hu said, "We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment." AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter's results. As reported by Tom's Hardware , Intel's Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel's revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD's business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs . Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Read full article Comments

title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
abstract: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide. One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects. In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US. Read full article Comments

title: After Texas' blue wave, what happens to Elon Musk and SpaceX?
abstract: Following his public disputes with California authorities during the COVID-19 pandemic, Elon Musk personally moved to Texas, outside of Austin, in 2020. Over the next six years, he doubled down on the Lone Star State. In 2021, Musk increasingly focused the Starship program in South Texas, urging SpaceX employees to move there and work on the company's future. In March of that year, he began using the name Starbase to describe the production and launch facilities near the Rio Grande River. In 2023, he built a massive factory east of Austin to manufacture customer terminals and other electronics for the Starlink program. In July 2024, he announced that SpaceX would relocate its corporate headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas. He cited California's regulatory and political environment as the motivating factor. Read full article Comments

title: Ted Cruz aims to stack FCC with Republicans before Democrats take Senate control
abstract: Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is aiming to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take over control of the Senate in January 2027. Just before the Republicans' midterm loss, Cruz yesterday announced a November 10 nomination hearing for Trump's FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs. In his final two months as chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, Cruz seems set on moving the Thumann Severs nomination to a full vote of the Senate. Confirming Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC. That could become a 3-0 advantage at the end of 2027 because FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would have to leave the commission at that time if Trump does not agree to renominate her. Read full article Comments

title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
abstract: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today's world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics. The company's cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it's probably "enough" for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. Specs at a glance: Enough Phone ($399 for a limited time, $599 MSRP) SoC MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Memory 8GB Storage 128GB with microSD Display 5.3-inch 1520x720 HD+ LCD Cameras Sony IMX766 50 MP, 32 MP selfie Software Android 17 or OdysseyOS Battery 3500 mAh (removable) Connectivity 5G, LTE, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, NFC, SIM+eSIM Measurements 133×64×12 mm With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it's a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you'll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off. Read full article Comments

title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
abstract: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments

title: What I learned driving the Slate electric truck prototype
abstract: If my 45-minute drive yesterday morning is anything to go by, I think Slate Auto will have quite the hit on its hands. The startup had one of its prototype trucks in town and asked if I wanted to check it out—no jumping on a plane or having to spend yet another night in an interchangeable hotel room, just a drive from southwest DC to Rockville, Maryland. Easy-peasy. The prototype truck had been well-used, with almost 6,000 miles (9,656 km) showing on the small and minimalist but very legible digital display that also shows your speed and, if you engage reverse, the backup camera. And while the cabin layout was representative of the production version, the surfaces most certainly weren’t—the prototype instead uses a lot of hard and shiny black plastic, with strips of Velcro here and there left over from when the interior had to be camouflaged when the vehicle was out in public. Getting acquainted with the Slate was refreshingly easy. The Morris Marina-like door handles open with a pleasing mechanical action. The seat and steering column adjust manually but with plenty of reach, something many budget models used to leave out to save on cost. Read full article Comments

title: The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle
abstract: In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain. Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die. Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms. Read full article Comments

title: California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws
abstract: California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations. California's stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects. Read full article Comments

title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
abstract: Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers. These consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex , the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance. Now, state-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti . The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage. Read full article Comments

title: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
abstract: The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies. "Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere," the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that "Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission," while "publishers have received nothing." The lawsuit said, "AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index," and use content from the Brave index "to train their own AI models" and "to respond to specific user queries." The NYT lawsuit points to Brave's website , which says the Brave Search API is "used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com." Read full article Comments

title: Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors
abstract: As with interior design for houses, interior design for vehicles is also subject to fashion trends. And like any fashion trend, even the best ideas can become stale and played out with overuse. Some ideas weren’t the best, either, like demonstrably worse human-machine interfaces that add to driver distraction; yet, they still proliferated throughout the industry and across the cars offered for sale. But the good news is that the pushback seems to be working. “When the trend of the Piano Black and the switchless interior was happening, it was during a time when designers and companies and engineers and everybody were thinking that, 'Hey, we can just get rid of all these switches on the interior. We can put it all in the software. It'll save money. It'll save us tooling up all these extra parts for unique cars and all this stuff and make the interior more like a software experience.' And it was done with those intentions,” said Hiren Patel, senior design manager at Nissan. That resulted in cars with minimalist interiors that looked good in the dealership. But people drive their cars on roads; they don’t just sit inside them, parked inside a dealership. “So lots of people were complaining about it and saying, 'Hey, it takes my eyes off the road to change the temperature or to adjust my seat or do whatever.' It's not as easy as doing something on your phone where it's just right at your fingertips and intuitive,” Patel said. Read full article Comments

title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
abstract: While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company's education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision. Google's new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months. When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search . There's no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it. Read full article Comments

title: Another child dies of measles as CDC reportedly holds up health alert
abstract: A child in New York has died of measles, health officials in the state announced late Monday . It marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in more than 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the US this year; all six of the other deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic measles outbreak that has stricken over 1,430 people this year . Prior to the deaths, Pennsylvania hadn't seen a measles-related death in 35 years. The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases, and tragic deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the US currently serves as the US health secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent decades prior to taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation. He and his anti-vaccine organization, Children's Health Defense, have been one of the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content . Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged , unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries ; and continuing to spread misinformation about vaccines and vaccine-preventable illnesses . Read full article Comments

title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
abstract: Google's Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to "obfuscation techniques" employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology. In a detailed blog post , the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong's compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online. After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator's behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious. Read full article Comments

title: This space company is betting its future on a propellant available everywhere
abstract: Robert, Ryan, and Kirby Carlisle are three engineers who worked at SpaceX during the Falcon 9 era, seeing the revolution in the global launch industry from the inside. The brothers launched rockets, refurbished rockets, and sold rockets. But when it came time for them to leave SpaceX and start their own space company—a lifetime dream for the Carlisle brothers—they chose not to build rockets. Rather, they focused on spacecraft. In late 2022, the three Carlisles founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. They chose water, which is potentially harvestable on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, as a means of propulsion. Read full article Comments

title: The Blue Wave Has Tech Bros Scrambling for Data Centers in Space
abstract: After Democrats won big in Texas and other AI infrastructure hot spots on Tuesday, data center enthusiasts looked for comfort in low Earth orbit.

title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms
abstract: Leading the Future, backed by Silicon Valley’s biggest billionaires, had a war chest of $100 million and an aggressive stance against AI regulation. All of it didn’t add up to much on Tuesday night.

title: Google Is Forcing AI Overviews in Classrooms. Schools Are Searching for a Way Out
abstract: Google is tying up AI Overviews with traditional search, angering parents and educators who worry that easy, machine-generated answers are leaving kids less capable.

title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
abstract: “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Clément Delangue said of the need for open source AI.

title: The Results Are In: Voters Hate Data Centers
abstract: From high-profile Senate races to local rezoning initiatives, data centers and their supporters did miserably on the ballot in the 2026 midterms.

title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
abstract: The AI minister now concedes the estimated figure is less than a third of that. Researchers blame the country’s slow rate of adoption.

title: Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote
abstract: From hallucinations to partisan bias, artificial intelligence chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are not helpful when it comes to Election Day.

title: ‘Our Risk, Their Reward’: Zohran Mamdani on AI and Data Centers
abstract: Ahead of the midterms, WIRED talked to New York City’s mayor about data centers, AI in schools, and the future of the Democratic party.

title: When You Should—and Shouldn’t—Use AI to Search the Web
abstract: Chatbots are often quite good at retrieving the information you want from the web. But sometimes you’ll get better results by typing your query into a good old search engine.

title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
abstract: WIRED uncovered some 400 apps and websites linked to Chinese-language developers that look like regular AI tools but had secret features that let users create violent AI-generated images and video.

title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - WebAssembly
abstract: 2020년 글 은 W3C 권고(1.0) 직후의 WebAssembly(이하 'wasm')를 다뤘습니다. '미래 버전에 포함될 작업'으로 스레드, SIMD(single instruction, multiple data), 참조 타입, 꼬리 호출, ESM(ECMAScript modules) 통합을 소개했고, Bytecode Alliance와 WASI(WebAssembly System Interface)가 그리는 브라우저 밖의 그림을 살펴봤습니다. 그리고 "아직까지 실서비스에서의 활발한 사용이 눈에 띄지는 않는다"라는 말과 함께, Sass가 wasm으로 플랫폼별 빌드 문제를 풀 수 있을지 모른다는 기대로 글을 맺었습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 이 글에서는 2020년 글 이후 6년을 이어서 정리합니다. 2020년에 예고했던 기능들의 결말, wasm 2.0과 3.0, 지금 진행 중인 제안, WasmGC 덕분에 웹에서 쓸 수 있게 된 언어들, Component Model과 WASI가 바꾼 브라우저 밖의 생태계, JavaScript 개발자가 알게 모르게 쓰고 있는 wasm 패키지들을 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 도구와 에이전트가 wasm의 쓰임새를 어떻게 바꾸고 있는지도 정리합니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2020년 이후 6년 2020년 글을 쓸 당시 wasm은 숫자 타입 네 가지( i32 , i64 , f32 , f64 )와 연속된 바이트 배열인 선형 메모리(linear memory)만 가진, 말 그대로 '컴파일 타깃'이었습니다. JavaScript와 문자열 하나를 주고받으려 해도 메모리에 바이트를 쓰고 그 위치를 숫자로 넘기는 글루 코드(glue code)가 필요했습니다. 6년이 지난 지금 wasm은 GC(가비지 컬렉션), 예외 처리, 64비트 주소 공간, 꼬리 호출을 명세에 담은 3.0이 되었습니다. Java, Kotlin, Dart 같은 GC 언어가 자체 런타임을 통째로 싣지 않고 wasm으로 컴파일됩니다. 브라우저 밖에서는 WASI가 Component Model 위로 옮겨 가며 0.2, 0.3이 나왔고, CDN 업체들이 wasm 기반 엣지 플랫폼을 운영하고 있습니다. 표 1 2019년 이후 주요 사건 시기 사건 2019년 12월 wasm 1.0 W3C 권고 2020년 10월 LibSass, Node Sass 비권장(deprecated) 지정 2023년 11월 V8 팀, WasmGC 포팅 가이드 공개(Chrome 119부터 WasmGC 지원) 2024년 1월 WASI 0.2 출시, WASI가 Component Model 기반으로 전환 2024년 6월 Google Sheets 계산 엔진의 WasmGC 전환 사례 공개 2024년 7월 Node Sass 지원 종료(end-of-life) 2024년 12월 W3C, wasm 2.0 후보 권고안 스냅샷 구현 요청 2025년 9월 wasm 3.0 발표 2025년 12월 Akamai, Fermyon 인수 발표 2026년 6월 WASI 0.3 출시, Safari 27 베타에서 JSPI(JS Promise Integration) 지원 Bytecode Alliance가 2026년 1월 발행한 10주년 회고 에 따르면, wasm은 2015년 6월 17일 4개 브라우저 벤더가 동시에 발표했고 2017년 말에 4대 브라우저가 모두 지원했습니다. 2019년 3월에 WASI가 발표되었고, 2024년 1월 WASI 0.2가 Component Model과 함께 나왔습니다. 2020년 '미래 버전에 포함될 작업'의 결말 2020년 글은 WebAssembly WG(Working Group)와 CG(Community Group)가 진행하던 작업으로 다섯 가지를 꼽았습니다. 6년이 지난 지금 다섯 항목 가운데 네 가지는 모든 주요 브라우저가 지원하지만, 명세상의 위치는 제각각입니다. 표 2 2020년에 소개한 기능의 현재 상태(2026년 10월 기준) 기능 명세상 위치 Chrome Firefox Safari 스레드 별도 제안(Phase 4) 74 79 14.1 128비트 SIMD wasm 2.0 91 89 16.4 참조 타입 wasm 2.0 96 79 15 꼬리 호출 wasm 3.0 112 121 18.2 ESM 통합 제안(Phase 3) 미지원 미지원 미지원 표 2의 브라우저 버전은 WebAssembly Feature Status 를, 제안의 단계는 WebAssembly/proposals 를 따랐습니다. 스레드 2020년 글은 Chrome 74부터 wasm 스레드가 기본 활성 상태라고 소개했습니다. 지금은 Firefox 79, Safari 14.1까지 지원 범위가 넓어졌습니다. 공유 메모리( SharedArrayBuffer )의 원자적 읽기와 쓰기, wait / notify 명령어로 구성된 이 제안 은 Phase 4(표준화 단계)에 있으며, 핵심 명세에는 아직 병합되지 않았습니다. 이 제안은 스레드 생성을 Web Workers에 맡기고, Emscripten 같은 툴체인이 이를 import로 노출하는 방식을 택했습니다. 공유 대상으로 정의한 것도 선형 메모리뿐이어서, 테이블, 전역 변수, WasmGC 객체는 스레드 사이에 공유할 수 없습니다. 이 한계를 다루는 후속 제안이 뒤에서 설명할 Shared-Everything Threads입니다. 128비트 SIMD 2020년 글에서 배열 4개 요소의 덧셈을 한 번의 CPU 명령으로 줄이는 예로 소개한 SIMD는 wasm 2.0에 Vector Instructions라는 이름으로 포함되었습니다. Chrome 91, Firefox 89, Safari 16.4부터 지원합니다(참고: Change History , WebAssembly Feature Status ). wasm 3.0에는 SIMD를 확장한 relaxed SIMD 가 추가되었습니다. 플랫폼별로 결과가 조금씩 다를 수 있는 연산(예: 융합 곱셈 덧셈)을 명세가 허용한 범위 안에서 하드웨어에 맞게 실행하도록 해 성능을 더 끌어냅니다. Chrome 114, Firefox 145에서 지원하고 Safari는 아직 플래그 뒤에 있습니다(참고: WebAssembly Feature Status ). 참조 타입 wasm 코드가 호스트 객체를 직접 참조하게 하는 참조 타입(reference types)은 wasm 2.0에 포함되었습니다. funcref 와 externref 두 가지 값 타입이 추가되었고, externref 로 JavaScript 객체를 wasm 쪽에서 숫자 인덱스로 바꾸지 않고 그대로 들고 있을 수 있게 되었습니다(참고: Change History ). 참조 타입은 이후 wasm 3.0의 typed function references와 GC의 바탕이 되었습니다. 꼬리 호출 추가 스택 공간을 쓰지 않고 함수를 호출하는 꼬리 호출(tail calls)은 wasm 3.0에 return_call , return_call_indirect 명령어로 포함되었습니다. 함수형 언어(Scheme, OCaml 등)의 컴파일러가 재귀를 반복문으로 바꾸는 우회 기법 없이 wasm을 생성할 수 있게 되었습니다(참고: Change History ). V8은 v11.2에서 꼬리 호출을 출시 했고, Emscripten으로 C++ 코루틴을 구현하는 사례를 함께 소개했습니다. 그림 1 꼬리 호출 시 호출자 프레임을 정리한 뒤 피호출 함수를 실행하는 스택 변화(출처: WebAssembly tail calls ) ESM 통합 다섯 항목 가운데 유일하게 아직 브라우저에 기본 탑재되지 않은 기능입니다. 제안은 Phase 3(구현 단계)에 있고, JavaScript 쪽 문법인 TC39의 Source Phase Imports도 Stage 3입니다(참고: WebAssembly/proposals , TC39 proposals ). 진행 상황은 뒤의 ' 진행 중인 제안 ' 절에서 자세히 설명합니다. wasm 2

title: 크림에서 통합 임베딩(Universal Embedding)은 어떻게 쓰일까?
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 크림에서 통합 임베딩(Universal Embedding)은 어떻게 쓰일까? NAVER D2 | 크림에서 통합 임베딩(Universal Embedding)은 어떻게 쓰일까? naver.me ​ 발표 내용 여러 엔티티를 한 공간에 담은 통합 임베딩과 범용 리트리벌이 크림 추천 곳곳에 쓰이는 방식, 운영하며 드러난 한계를 v2에서 해결한 과정, 그리고 확장 방향을 공유합니다. ​ 발표 대상 추천 시스템의 후보 생성(Retrieval) 단계에 관심 있으신 분들 여러 서비스·지면에서 함께 쓰는 공용 임베딩을 설계하고 운영하고 싶으신 ML 엔지니어 조건(필터)이 걸린 벡터 검색의 지연과 메모리를 줄이고 싶으신 분들 구좌·서비스마다 늘어나는 추천 모델을 줄이고 싶은 추천·검색 조직의 엔지니어와 기획자 ​ 키워드 Recommendation System / Candidate Generation (Retrieval) Universal Embedding (Bi-encoder · Contrastive Learning) Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) Filtered Vector Retrieval (Roaring Bitmap · Brute-force vs ANN) Embedding Serving Optimization ​ 목차 PART 1. 왜 통합 임베딩인가 2025년의 크림: 추천 구좌마다 모델이 따로 있었다 목표: 여러 목적에 쓸 수 있는 범용 임베딩 하나 구좌마다 ‘누구에게 · 무엇을 · 어떻게’가 다르다 통합 임베딩은 후보 생성에 직접, 랭킹에도 입력으로 설계 원칙: 모든 질문이 ‘벡터 + 조건’이 된다 PART 2. v1 모델 — 하나의 공간을 만들다 하나의 인코더가 검색어와 상품을 모두 읽는다 학습: InfoNCE를 받쳐 주는 일곱 가지 장치 학습은 상품 하나, 나머지는 모두 집계로 그림으로 보면: 모두가 상품 공간 위의 점 PART 3. v1 리트리벌 — 하나의 API로 꺼내 쓰다 질문 하나 = 요청 하나 조건별 상품 목록을 미리 만들어 두고 꺼내 쓰기 구좌 전용 모델 없이 붙은 첫 구좌들과 타겟 집단 추천 PART 4. 써 보니 드러난 v1의 한계 모델: 가끔 붕괴하고, 768차원은 무거웠다 리트리벌: 큰 조건을 감당하지 못했다 리트리벌: 조건을 자유롭게 조합할 수 없었다 v1의 한계, 한눈에 PART 5. v2 — 한계를 하나씩 걷어내다 모델 1차: 학습을 안정시키다 모델 2차: 하나의 벡터, 여러 해상도 (MRL) 좌표계: 회전으로 맞추려 했지만, 통하지 않았다 필터: Roaring Bitmap으로 조건을 실행할 때 조합 왜 근사 검색(ANN)이 아니라 후보 전부를 계산하나 점수 계산: 계산량은 그대로, 메모리 낭비만 없앴다 결과: 응답 지연은 약 4배 빠르게, 메모리는 1/6로 API: 조건 칸 하나 → 조건 리스트 v1의 한계 → v2의 처방 PART 6. 지금의 쓰임과 다음 확장 지금: 하나의 API가 채우는 지면과 구좌 비슷한 브랜드: 브랜드 벡터만으로는 부족했다 리트리벌 밖에서도 같은 벡터 다음으로 — 멀티벡터, 지면 확장, 마케팅 타겟팅 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: FE News 26년 11월 소식을 전해드립니다.
abstract: 주요소식 26년 11월 소식에서는 다음과 같은 유용한 정보들을 만나보실 수 있습니다. ​ Tailwind Labs is joining Shopify Tailwind CSS를 만든 Adam Wathan이 Tailwind Labs의 Shopify 합류를 발표했다. Tailwind CSS를 비롯한 오픈소스 프로젝트는 계속 MIT 라이선스로 남고 Tailwind 팀이 Shopify의 지원을 받아 유지보수를 이어 가므로, 이미 쓰고 있는 팀이 당장 바꿀 것은 없다. 대신 유료 컴포넌트·템플릿 모음 Tailwind Plus와 에이전트 스킬 모음 ui.sh는 신규 가입을 받지 않으며, Wathan은 사용자와 같은 문제를 겪는 실제 커머스 제품 안에서 프레임워크를 개발하고 싶었다고 배경을 설명한다. ​ ​ ​ Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust Cloudflare와 VoidZero가 TypeScript 컴파일러를 Rust로 옮기는 tsrs를 Oxc 툴체인 안에서 개발한다고 발표했다. Go로 다시 작성한 TypeScript 7보다 WebAssembly 환경에 잘 맞고 메모리를 적게 쓰는 것이 목표로, 팀의 초기 벤치마크에서는 TypeScript 7.0보다 최대 8배 빠르고 메모리를 약 70% 덜 썼다. 비슷한 시기에 나온 ts-rust, Bun의 bun check, Vercel Labs의 tsc-ts도 함께 소개하며, 모두 실험 단계이므로 CI 타입 검사가 병목인 팀이라면 기존 tsc와 진단 결과를 비교하며 시험해 볼 만하다. ​ ​ ​ Making React Context Cheap with React Compiler Context 값이 바뀌면 그 Context를 읽는 모든 컴포넌트가 다시 렌더링되는 비용을 React Compiler로 줄이는 방법을 다룬 글이다. 라디오 버튼 5,000개 예제에서 컴포넌트를 나누지 않고 Context를 그대로 읽게 둔 채 메모이제이션을 React Compiler에 맡기면, 클릭 처리 시간이 useSyncExternalStore 스토어나 React.memo로 나눈 방식과 비슷한 수준이 된다. 저자는 렌더링 횟수보다 렌더링 한 번의 작업량이 사용자 체감을 좌우한다며, 렌더링을 없애기보다 싸게 만드는 데 집중하라고 권한다. ​ ​ ​ React 19.3 실험 단계였던 <ViewTransition>과 Fragment Refs가 안정화되었다. <ViewTransition>은 Transition으로 표시된 업데이트에서 요소의 등장, 퇴장, 갱신에 View Transition API 애니메이션을 적용하고, Fragment Refs로는 래퍼 요소 없이 형제 DOM 노드 묶음에 이벤트 리스너나 Observer를 연결할 수 있다. 컴포넌트를 서버 렌더링에서 제외하는 browser() API와 Trusted Types 지원도 추가되었으며, Strict Mode가 하이드레이션 중에도 Effect를 두 번 실행하므로 업그레이드 후에는 정리 함수가 없는 Effect부터 점검해 둬야 한다. ​ ​ ​ Remix 3 Remix 3이 Remix Jam 2026에 맞춰 첫 안정 버전으로 출시되었다. remix 패키지 하나에 라우터, 데이터베이스 관리, 스키마 검증, 에셋 서버, React가 아닌 자체 UI 런타임을 담은 풀스택 프레임워크이며, 기존 Remix 2 앱은 Remix 3이 아니라 React Router로 옮기게 된다. 10월 23일 나온 3.1은 코드 변경 없이 서버 렌더링을 약 두 배 빠르게 했고, 팀은 정식 출시 이후 SemVer를 지키겠다고 밝혔다. ​ ​ ​ >> FE News 26년 11월 소식 보러가기 ◎ FE News란? 네이버 FE 엔지니어들이 엄선한 양질의 FE 및 주요한 기술 소식들을 큐레이션해 공유하는 것을 목표로 하며, 이를 통해 국내 개발자들에게 지식 공유에 대한 가치 인식과 성장에 도움을 주고자 하는 기술소식 공유 프로젝트 입니다. 매월 첫째 주 수요일, 월 1회 발행 되고 있으니 많은 관심 부탁드립니다. ▷ 구독하기

title: 딸깍으로 안되는 Multi-interest 개발기
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ 딸깍으로 안되는 Multi-interest 개발기 NAVER D2 | 딸깍으로 안되는 Multi-interest 개발기 naver.me ​ 발표 내용 다양한 관심사 추천 모델인 Multi-interest를 여러 지면에 적용하며 겪었던 문제를 해결했던 과정을 공유합니다. ​ 주제: Multi-interest 추천 모델(MINER)의 KREAM 실서비스 적용 사례 문제: 인기 상품 목록에서 특정 상품이 전체 유저에게 동시 노출되는 hubness 발생 분석: 점수를 유저 의존 성분과 유저 무관 성분으로 분해, 가설 3개를 실측으로 검증 조치: 유저 무관 성분 제거(centering, bias 분리), 추천 결과 다양화, 분포 지표 기반 평가 체계 도입 결과: 과노출 상품 전량 제거, 노출 상품 종류 +25%, 구매 지표 유지 시사점: 논문 구조의 실서비스 적용 시 발생하는 문제와 사전 점검 항목 ​ 발표 대상 Multi-interest 추천 모델에 관심 있으신 분들 ​ 목차 문제상황 가설 수립, 유저 의존 성분 + 유저 무관 성분 전략 1. 유저 무관 성분 낮추기 전략 2. 유저 유관 성분 높이기 전략 3. 두 성분을 지표에서 모니터링 남은 과제 및 점검항목 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다.

title: 컨테이너처럼 쓰고, VM처럼 격리하기
abstract: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 컨테이너처럼 쓰고, VM처럼 격리하기: kata-containers with GPU NAVER D2 | 컨테이너처럼 쓰고, VM처럼 격리하기: kata-containers with GPU naver.me ​ 발표 내용 Kubernetes GPU 노드를 VM으로 격리해 나눠 쓰면서, 호스트 수준의 성능까지 최적화한 방법을 소개합니다. ​ 발표 대상 여러 사용자가 GPU node를 함께 쓰는 환경에서 격리를 강화하려는 플랫폼 개발자 Kubernetes에서 kata-containers나 VM 기반 runtime 도입을 검토하는 개발자 DRA로 GPU·NIC 같은 device 할당을 직접 구현하려는 개발자 VM 환경에서 GPU·IB·storage 성능을 bare metal 수준으로 맞추려는 개발자 ​ 발표자료 국문 영문 ​ 목차 도입 배경과 kata-containers의 구조 GPU와 NIC를 VM에 함께 할당하기 VM 부팅 시간과 성능 개선하기 마무리: 사용자가 작성하는 Pod spec과 bare metal 대비 성능 ​ ◎ NAVER Engineering Day란? ​ NAVER에서는 사내 개발 경험과 기술 트렌드를 교류를 할 수 있는 프로그램이 많이 있습니다. 그중 이제는 매회 평균 100개 이상의 발표가 이루어지는 NAVER Engineering Day를 빼놓을 수 없는데요. 2016년부터 시작된 ENGINEERING DAY는 실무에서의 기술 개발 경험과 새로운 기술과 플랫폼 도입 시 유용하게 활용될 수 있는 팁 등을 공유하며 서로 배우고 성장하는 네이버의 대표적인 사내 개발자 행사입니다.( 관련 포스팅 보기 ) 올해 진행된 NAVER Engineering Day의 일부 세션을 공개합니다. ​ [동영상 제공 채널 안내] 네이버 TV 서비스 종료로 인해 기존 네이버 TV 채널을 클립( @devrel_d2 )으로 이동하였습니다. 앞으로도 많은 관심과 팔로우 부탁드리겠습니다. ​ ​

title: FE News 26년 10월 소식을 전해드립니다.
abstract: 주요소식 ​ The Story of VS Code Visual Studio Code 공식 채널이 공개한 약 1시간 38분 분량의 다큐멘터리로, Erich Gamma가 이끈 취리히 팀이 브라우저용 편집기 컴포넌트 Monaco Editor를 만들던 시기부터 데스크톱 VS Code 발표와 오픈 소스 전환까지의 과정을 30여 명의 관계자 인터뷰로 보여 준다. 확장을 별도 프로세스에서 실행하고 한번 공개한 API는 바꾸지 않는 원칙, TypeScript 서버에서 출발한 LSP, UI와 확장 호스트를 분리한 구조가 원격 개발과 vscode.dev로 이어진 배경을 설명한다. 후반부에서는 GitHub Copilot의 출발과 Ask, Edits, Agent Mode로 이어진 AI 기능, Cursor 같은 포크를 바라보는 VS Code 팀의 시각도 소개한다. ​ ​ Native is now the future of mobile at Shopify 2020년 React Native 전면 도입을 선언했던 Shopify가 모바일 앱을 다시 Swift와 Kotlin 네이티브로 옮긴다고 발표했다. 코딩 에이전트 덕분에 두 플랫폼에 각각 구현하는 비용이 줄면서 공유 구현보다 네이티브의 이점이 커졌다는 판단으로, Shop 앱은 12주 만에 재구축했고 화면을 작은 체크포인트로 나눠 테스트, 시각 비교, 적대적 코드 리뷰, 사람의 승인을 거치게 하는 Helix 시스템을 만들었다. React Native Skia, FlashList, Restyle 등 Shopify가 관리해 온 오픈소스의 향후 계획도 공개해, 이 라이브러리를 쓰는 프로젝트라면 전환 일정을 확인해 둬야 한다. ​ ​ 토스 FE 개발자들의 검증법 토스 웨비나에서 Front AI 팀이 AI로 만든 결과물을 검증하는 방법을 소개한 세션이다. 코드에서 시나리오를 추론해 E2E 테스트를 자동 생성하려던 시도가 실패한 뒤, 얼굴 인식 결제처럼 실수 비용이 큰 영역에서 테스트를 직접 작성하며 디바이스 팜 조작 도구, 액션 로그 조회 스킬처럼 테스트를 막던 요소를 해결하는 도구를 만들어 온 과정을 설명한다. 사람이 CI 실패 원인을 파악하도록 만든 replay 도구를 에이전트에 그대로 넘기자 버튼 문구 변경 같은 실패를 스스로 고쳤다는 경험은 AI 검증 체계를 고민하는 FE 팀이 참고할 만하다 . ​ ​ penpot 브라우저에서 쓰거나 직접 설치해 운영할 수 있는 오픈소스 디자인, 프로토타이핑 플랫폼이다. 디자인을 SVG, CSS, HTML 같은 개방형 표준으로 표현하고 CSS Grid와 Flex 레이아웃, 디자인 토큰, 컴포넌트를 기본 기능으로 제공하며, MCP 서버를 통해 Cursor나 Claude Code 같은 AI 에이전트가 컴포넌트, 토큰, 레이어 구조를 읽고 수정할 수 있다. 셀프 호스팅이 가능해 디자인 데이터를 사내에 두어야 하는 조직이 검토해 볼 만한 MPL-2.0 라이선스 프로젝트다. ​ Full Course: Spec-Driven Development with Coding Agents DeepLearning.AI와 JetBrains가 만든 명세 주도 개발(Spec-Driven Development) 강좌의 전체 영상으로, 마크다운 명세를 먼저 쓰고 코딩 에이전트가 이를 구현하게 하는 흐름을 WebStorm과 Claude Code로 Next.js 예제 앱을 만들며 보여 준다. mission.md, techstack.md, roadmap.md로 프로젝트 헌장을 만든 뒤 기능마다 명세를 작성하고 컨텍스트를 비운 상태에서 구현을 맡기는 반복 과정을 설명한다. 기존 코드베이스에서 헌장을 역으로 만드는 방법과 Spec Kit, OpenSpec 같은 공개 SDD 도구도 소개해, 코딩 에이전트 결과물의 일관성을 고민하는 개발자에게 도움이 된다. ​ ​ >> FE News 26년 10월 소식 보러가기 ◎ FE News란? 네이버 FE 엔지니어들이 엄선한 양질의 FE 및 주요한 기술 소식들을 큐레이션해 공유하는 것을 목표로 하며, 이를 통해 국내 개발자들에게 지식 공유에 대한 가치 인식과 성장에 도움을 주고자 하는 기술소식 공유 프로젝트 입니다. 매월 첫째 주 수요일, 월 1회 발행 되고 있으니 많은 관심 부탁드립니다. ▷ 구독하기

title: 옮기는 것보다 증명이 어렵다
abstract: 클레임 검색 색인의 CDC 전환과 검증 기록 요약 커머스 클레임(취소·교환·반품) 검색 색인의 변경 수집 방식을 변경 알림 기반에서 데이터베이스 변경 로그 기반, 즉 CDC로 전환했습니다. 기존 구조에서는 알림이 발행되지 않은 변경이 색인에 반영되지 않았고, 건의 체류 시간을 계산하는 기준시각이 무관한 필드 수정에 갱신되는 문제가 있었습니다. 전환보다 어려웠던 작업은 새 색인이 맞다는 것을 보이는 일이었습니다. 누락·값·지연 세 축으로 대조한 결과, 보...

title: 국내 최초 광고 MCP를 출시하며, 개발자의 역할은 어디까지 넓어졌을까?
abstract: 안녕하세요. 당근 광고실 광고주플랫폼팀에서 백엔드 엔지니어로 일하는 제이크(Jake)예요. 얼마 전 저희 팀 엔지니어링 매니저 Iltaek이 프론트엔드와 백엔드를 한 팀으로 합친 이야기 를 글로 나눴어요. 그 글이 팀의 경계를 넘어 일하는 이야기였다면, 이번 글은 제가 당근 광고 MCP를 만들며 개발자의 역할을 넓혀 본 이야기 예요. MCP(Model Context Protocol)는 AI 서비스가 외부 서비스의 데이터를 불러올 때 쓰는 표준 연결 방식이에요. 광고주가 Claude 같은 AI 서비스에 “지난주 광고 성과 어땠어?”라고 물으면, AI가 광고 MCP를 거쳐 당근 광고의 계정 정보와 광고 정보, 성과 데이터를 가져와서 답해 줘요. 해외 광고 플랫폼에서는 구글, 메타, 아마존이 이미 MCP를 공개했고, 국내에서는 당근이 처음으로 공식 광고 MCP를 출시했어요. 저는 개발자로 이 프로젝트에 참여하는 줄 알았는데, 하다 보니 로드맵과 PRD부터 출시까지 맡아야 했어요. 이 글에서는 그 과정에서 겪은 일과, 제가 일하는 방식이 어떻게 달라졌는지 이야기해 보려고 해요. 로드맵과 PRD를 처음 써 봤어요 그동안은 PM과 함께 일하면서 엔지니어로서 개발에 필요한 의견을 나누고, PRD를 어떻게 구현할지 고민했어요. 그런데 이번에는 Iltaek에게 로드맵과 PRD까지 맡아 달라는 요청을 받았어요. 솔직히 요청을 받았을 때는 “이것도 개발자인 내 일인가?” 싶었어요. 로드맵은 PM이 그리는 거 아닌가, 내가 로드맵을 제시하는 게 맞나 하는 생각이 먼저 들었어요. 해 본 적 없는 일이라 부담도 됐고요. 그때 Iltaek이 오너라는 마음가짐으로 해 보라고 했어요. 그 말대로 “내 프로젝트”라고 생각하다 보니, 이 프로젝트를 더 잘되게 하려면 뭘 해야 할지 고민하게 되더라고요. 스스로 던지는 질문부터 달라졌어요. 로드맵을 그리려고 하니, 당근 광고 플랫폼은 생각보다 크고 복잡했어요. 전문가모드, 간편모드, 대행사 플랫폼¹까지 합치면 광고주가 할 수 있는 일이 정말 많아요. 광고 보고서, 광고 수정, 소재 만들기, 타겟팅, 전환 추적, 결제와 충전까지요. 이걸 한 번에 다 MCP로 열 수는 없어서, 범위를 좁혀야 했어요. 혹시나 잘못되더라도 광고주에게 손해가 없는 일인지, 화면보다 AI로 했을 때 더 편한 일인지, 더 많은 광고주에게 도움이 되는 일인지, 이렇게 세 가지 기준을 세워 봤어요. 그래서 리스크가 가장 낮은 조회 기능부터 열었어요. 광고를 수정하는 기능은 충분히 검증한 뒤에 열기로 했어요. AI가 예산이나 입찰가를 바꾸다 실수하면 광고비가 의도와 다르게 나갈 수 있어서요. 결제나 광고 삭제처럼 AI로 하는 게 오히려 불편하거나 위험한 일은 아예 열지 않기로 했어요. 그리고 당근 광고에서 가장 많이 집행되는 디스플레이 광고부터 시작했어요. 그렇게 로드맵을 그리고, 그 안에서 이번에 할 일의 범위를 정했어요. 그다음 저희 팀에서 쓰는 PTBSMAF라는 프레임워크로 PRD를 썼어요. 문제 정의(Problem Statement), 트레이드오프(Trade-off), 벤치마크(Benchmark), 해결책(Solution), 지표(Metrics), 중단 조건(Andon), 피드백 루프(Feedback Loop)의 앞 글자를 딴 이름이에요. 그중에서도 문제 정의, 트레이드오프, 벤치마크가 특히 도움이 됐어요. 문제를 제가 이해한 대로 풀어 쓰다 보니 생각이 정리됐고, 조회만 먼저 열면 무엇을 얻고 무엇을 포기하는지 적으면서 트레이드오프가 분명해졌어요. 특히 벤치마크에서는 다른 광고 플랫폼의 사례를 찾아보면서, 그대로 참고할 부분과 우리 상황에 맞게 바꿔야 할 부분이 구분됐어요. PRD를 쓰면서 이전에는 생각해 보지 못했던 부분까지 고민하게 됐어요. 이 기능으로 플랫폼이 무엇을 얻을지, 어느 제품부터 고려할지, 뭐가 더 나은 방향인지 같은 제품 관점의 고민은 전부 처음이었어요. 이렇게 정한 것들이 정답인지 100% 확신할 수는 없었지만, 적어도 근거를 가지고 정했다는 점은 지금 돌아봐도 만족스러워요. 로드맵은 PM이 그리는 거라고 생각했던 것도, 해 보고 나니 제 선입견이었던 것 같아요. API를 그대로 옮기면 될 줄 알았어요 로드맵과 PRD로 무엇을 하고 무엇을 하지 않을지 정하고 나니, 이제 도구를 어떻게 만들지 고민할 차례였어요. 광고주센터 뒤에는 이미 잘 돌아가는 API가 있어서, 그걸 MCP 도구로 하나씩 감싸기만 하면 될 거라고 생각했어요. 그런데 API를 그대로 도구로 만들면, AI가 어떤 도구를 써야 할지 헷갈려하고, 필요한 정보를 놓쳐 잘못된 답을 할 수 있더라고요. 예를 들어 광고주가 “이 광고 왜 안 나가?”라고 물었다고 해 볼게요. 광고주센터였다면 광고 정보, 노출 상태, 심사 결과가 한 화면에 같이 보였을 거예요. 그런데 API마다 도구를 따로 만들면, AI가 그중 뭘 부를지 스스로 골라야 해요. 광고 정보만 보고 “켜져 있으니 괜찮아요”라고 답하면서, 광고 심사에서 막힌 건 놓치는 식이에요. 메타 광고 MCP를 직접 연결해 보니, 도구가 많고 설명 방식도 제각각이라 AI가 광고주의 요청을 다르게 이해하는 경우가 있었어요. 로드맵을 그리며 광고주가 AI에게 무엇을 물어볼지 고민했던 게 여기서 도움이 됐어요. API를 그대로 옮기는 대신, 광고주의 질문을 기준으로 도구를 설계하기로 했어요. 그렇게 정리해 보니 좋은 API와 좋은 도구의 기준은 꽤 달랐어요. 이 기준으로, 가장 흔한 요청인 “지난주 성과 분석해 줘”를 예시로 도구를 설계해 봤어요. 이 요청은 어느 계정인지 정하고, 대상을 찾고, 성과를 보는 세 단계로 나눌 수 있어요. 그래서 단계마다 도구를 하나씩 두고 광고주센터 뒤의 여러 API를 3개의 도구로 정리했어요. 앞으로 광고 수정처럼 기능이 늘어나면 도구도 함께 늘어나겠지만, 그때도 이 기준을 지켜 가려고 해요. 제품으로 내놓으려면 챙길 게 많았어요 도구를 다 만들었다고 바로 내놓을 수 있는 건 아니었어요. AI가 광고주의 계정을 대신 다룰 수 있도록 약관을 검토하고 법무팀의 확인을 받아야 했어요. 기존 서버에 부하가 가지 않도록 적절한 호출 한도를 정해야 했고, 광고주용 연결 가이드와 서비스 내 안내 화면도 준비해야 했어요. 그리고 출시 후 운영을 위한 대시보드도 만들어야 했어요. 처음에는 좀 막막했어요. 일정을 챙기고, 회의를 잡고, 다른 팀과 일정을 맞추는 일은 개발자인 저에게 익숙하지 않았으니까요. 그럴 때마다 함께 진행한 PM인 Moana와 이야기하면서 하나씩 풀어 나갔어요. 챙길 일 중에서도 가장 걱정했던 건 인증 이었어요. MCP는 인증 방식이 표준으로 정해져 있어요. OAuth 2.1을 따라야 하고, MCP를 연결할 때 광고주 본인의 동의를 거쳐야 해요. 사내에서만 쓰는 게 아니라 외부 광고주에게 공개하려면, 이러한 표준을 반드시 지원해야 했어요. 다행히 당근의 인증을 맡고 있는 Identity Service Team에서 이미 SSO(Single Sign-On)를 제공하고 있었어요.² 그래서 MCP 인증도 지원해 달라고 요청드렸고, 인증 서버를 표준에 맞게 고쳐 주셨어요. 그리고 나서 광고 MCP에 인증 서버를 연동하고 AI 서비스에 연결해 봤어요. 그런데 OpenAI의 Codex에서는 로그인을 누르면 에러가 뜨고 그대로 끊겼어요. OpenAI 문서에는 이 표준을 지원한다고 나와 있어서 더 당황했는데, 알고 보니 그때 이 인증 방식에 대한 지원은 Codex 정식 버전에는 아직 들어가지 않았고 알파 버전에만 막 들어온 참이었어요. 이대로 출시하면 Codex에서는 광고 MCP를 연결할 수 없는 상황이었어요. 그래서 틈날 때마다 새 버전이 나왔는지 들여다봤어요. 출시 전에 정식 버전에서도 지원하게 돼서, 그제야 한숨 돌렸어요. 그렇게 9월 16일, 광고 MCP를 공개 베타로 출시했어요. 출시 후엔 광고주가 어떻게 쓰는지 궁금했어요 원래라면 개발하고 QA하고 프로덕션에 배포하면 끝났다고 생각했을 것 같아요. 그런데 제품을 맡고 보니, 배포하고 나서 의도한 대로 동작하는지가 궁금했어요. 광고주들이 이걸 실제로 어떻게 쓰는지, 어떻게 하면 더 잘 쓰게 할 수 있을지 계속 고민하게 됐어요. 그래서 도구가

title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories.
